'''George Michael Sheldrick''', [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (17 November 1942 – 20 February 2025) was a British chemist who specialised in [[molecular structure]] determination.<ref name=CV>{{cite web|title=CV|url=http://shelx.uni-ac.gwdg.de/~gsheldr/cvengl.pdf|access-date=15 November 2015|archive-date=17 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117023124/http://shelx.uni-ac.gwdg.de/~gsheldr/cvengl.pdf}}</ref> He was one of the most cited workers in the field, having over 280,000 citations as of 2020 and an [[h-index]] of 113.<ref>{{cite web|title=Google Scholar: George M. Sheldrick|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=7sHztskAAAAJ&hl=en|access-date=15 November 2015|archive-date=29 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160429080622/https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=7sHztskAAAAJ&hl=en}}</ref> He was a professor at the [[University of Göttingen]] from 1978 until his retirement in 2011.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chemistryviews.org/details/ezine/3608141/70th_Birthday_George_Sheldrick.html|title=70th Birthday: George Sheldrick|date=17 November 2012 |publisher=ChemistryViews.org|access-date=15 November 2015}}</ref>

==Early life==
Sheldrick was born on 17 November 1942 in [[Huddersfield]], England. He was educated at [[Huddersfield New College]], then an all-boys [[grammar school]]. He completed nine [[O-Levels]], six [[A-Levels]], and two [[S-Levels]]. At A-Level, he achieved a distinction (the highest [[Grading (education)|grade]]) in chemistry, mathematics and physics.<ref name=CV />

Sheldrick was awarded a Major Scholarship to study [[Natural Sciences (Cambridge)|Natural Sciences]] at [[Jesus College, Cambridge]]. He specialised in [[chemistry]] in his final year. He graduated in 1963 with a [[first class honours|first class]] Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree. He remained at the [[University of Cambridge]] to undertake [[postgraduate research]] under the [[Doctoral supervisor|supervision]] of [[Evelyn Ebsworth]]. He completed his Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) degree in 1966. The topic of his thesis was the investigation of [[Inorganic chemistry|inorganic]] [[hydrides]] using [[nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy]], and was titled "''N.M.R. Studies of Inorganic Hydrides''".<ref name=CV />

==Academic career==
In 1966, Sheldrick was elected a [[Fellow#Oxford, Cambridge and Dublin|Fellow]] of [[Jesus College, Cambridge]]. During his time as an academic at the [[University of Cambridge]], he also taught within the Faculty of Chemistry. He was a [[Academic ranks in the United Kingdom|demonstrator]] from 1966 to 1971, and a lecturer from 1971 to 1978.<ref name=CV />

Sheldrick joined the [[University of Göttingen]] in 1978. There, he was first [[Professor (highest academic rank)|Professor]] of [[Inorganic Chemistry]], then later Professor of [[Structural Chemistry]]. In 2011, he retired from full-time academia and was appointed Niedersachsen Professor (IE [[Emeritus Professor]]).<ref name=CV />

==Work==
Sheldrick dealt with molecular structure elucidation by X-ray diffraction. He was the lead developer of the [[SHELX]] program suite,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Sheldrick|first1=George M.|title=A short history of SHELX|journal=Acta Crystallographica Section A|date=21 December 2007|volume=64|issue=1|pages=112–122|doi=10.1107/S0108767307043930|pmid=18156677|doi-access=free}}</ref> which is freely available online.<ref>{{cite web|title=The SHELX homepage|url=http://shelx.uni-ac.gwdg.de/SHELX/index.php|access-date=15 November 2015}}</ref> In 2011, a graphical user interface for SHELX refinements called [[ShelXle]] was released.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hübschle|first1=Christian B.|last2=Sheldrick|first2=George M.|last3=Dittrich|first3=Birger|title=ShelXle: a Qt graphical user interface for SHELX|journal=Journal of Applied Crystallography|date=12 November 2011|volume=44|issue=6|pages=1281–1284|doi=10.1107/S0021889811043202|pmid=22477785|pmc=3246833|bibcode=2011JApCr..44.1281H }}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
On 13 July 1968, Sheldrick married Katherine Elizabeth Herford. Together they had four children.<ref name=CV /> He died on 20 February 2025, at the age of 82.<ref>[https://dgk-home.de/en/dgknews/nachruf-prof-george-m-sheldrick/ Obituary Prof. George M. Sheldrick]</ref>

His younger brother, William S. Sheldrick (1945–2015), was a professor of analytical chemistry at [[Ruhr University]] in [[Bochum]], Germany until his retirement in 2010.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Seidel|first1=Rüdiger W.|title=William S. Sheldrick (1945–2015)|journal=Zeitschrift für anorganische und allgemeine Chemie|date=April 2015|volume=641|issue=5|page=750|doi=10.1002/zaac.201510005|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Honours==
*1970 [[Meldola Medal]] of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]
*1978 [[Corday-Morgan Prize]] of the Royal Society of Chemistry
*1988 [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize]] of the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft
*1999 [[Carl-Hermann Medal]] of the [[German Society for Crystallography]]
*2001 [[Fellow of the Royal Society]]
*2004 [[Max Perutz Prize]] of the [[European Crystallographic Association]]
*2009 [[Gregori Aminoff Prize]] of the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences]]
*2011 [[Ewald Prize]] of the [[International Union of Crystallography]]
*2024 [[George M. Sheldrick Prize]] The [[European Crystallographic Association]] awarded its first award in honour of George Sheldrick.
